summary.text: Assuming the first claimed identity, the shifted pairs \((a_n+1,a_{n+1}+1)\) evolve by the Fibonacci matrix; a modular exponentiation modulo \(195318521017\), starting from the computed residues at indices 3773 and 3774, shows that after \(249580073233\) steps two consecutive terms are both divisible by this modulus. If their gcd is \(g\ge2\) and their sum is \(s=gq\) with \(q\ge2\), the defining recurrence gives the next term as \(g+q\), whereas the claimed identity gives \(1+gq\), impossible because \(1+gq-(g+q)=(g-1)(q-1)>0\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be the sequence defined by
\[
a_1=a_2=1,
\qquad
a_n=g_n+\frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}}{g_n}\quad(n\geq3),
\]
where
\[
g_n=\gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}).
\]
We will prove that it is impossible for even the first of the three conjectured formulas,
\[
 a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}, \tag{1}
\]
to hold for every \(n\geq3775\). This suffices to disprove the stated conjunction of all three formulas.

The proof uses the modulus
\[
P=195318521017.
\]
All matrix congruences below are taken modulo \(P\). Put
\[
Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

First we obtain the required initial residues directly from the defining recurrence. A convenient way to organize this finite calculation is to iterate the map
\[
T(r,s)=\left(s,\;\gcd(r,s)+\frac{r+s}{\gcd(r,s)}\right).
\]
An immediate induction on \(k\) shows that
\[
T^k(1,1)=(a_{k+1},a_{k+2}). \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, this is true at \(k=0\), and applying \(T\) replaces the consecutive pair \((a_{k+1},a_{k+2})\) by \((a_{k+2},a_{k+3})\), exactly by the defining recurrence.

Exact iteration through \(k=3772\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{3773}={}&,\\
a_{3774}={}&.
\end{aligned}
\]
Reducing these two integers modulo \(P\) gives
\[
a_{3773}\equiv77940394258\pmod P,
\qquad
a_{3774}\equiv99768150821\pmod P. \tag{3}
\]
Thus, after shifting each term by \(1\), the initial residue vector is
\[
v_0= inom{77940394259}{99768150822}. \tag{4}
\]

Now suppose, for contradiction, that (1) holds for every \(n\geq3775\). Adding \(1\) to (1) and regrouping yields
\[
a_n+1=(a_{n-2}+1)+(a_{n-1}+1). \tag{5}
\]
Consequently, if
\[
w_k= inom{a_{3773+k}+1}{a_{3774+k}+1},
\]
then for every \(k\geq0\), equation (5), applied at \(n=3775+k\), gives
\[
w_{k+1}=Qw_k. \tag{6}
\]
The base vector \(w_0\) is congruent to \(v_0\) by (3). Induction in (6) therefore gives
\[
w_k\equiv Q^k v_0\pmod P \qquad(k\geq0). \tag{7}
\]

We next perform a finite modular exponentiation. Set
\[
K=249580073233.
\]
Repeated squaring modulo \(P\) gives
\[
Q^K\equiv
\begin{pmatrix}
117378126758&21827756563\\
21827756563&139205883321
\end{pmatrix}. \tag{8}
\]

This proves (8) using only ordinary modular matrix multiplication.

Multiplying the final matrix in (8) by the vector (4), its first coordinate before reduction is
\[
117378126758\cdot77940394259
 +21827756563\cdot99768150822
 =11326212385784681827108.
\]
This equals
\[
57988419771\,P+1.
\]
Its second coordinate is
\[
21827756563\cdot77940394259
 +139205883321\cdot99768150822
 =15589577514788957011679,
\]
which equals
\[
79816176334\,P+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
Q^K v_0\equiv\binom11\pmod P. \tag{9}
\]
Combining (7) and (9), we find
\[
a_{3773+K}+1\equiv1\pmod P,
\qquad
a_{3774+K}+1\equiv1\pmod P.
\]
After subtracting \(1\), this says
\[
P\mid a_{3773+K}
\quad\text{and}\quad
P\mid a_{3774+K}. \tag{10}
\]

Let
\[
x=a_{3773+K},\qquad y=a_{3774+K},
\qquad g=\gcd(y,x),\qquad s=x+y.
\]
Because \(K\geq2\), both indices \(3773+K\) and \(3774+K\) are at least \(3775\). Under the assumed recurrence (1), each of \(x\) and \(y\) is of the form \(1\) plus a sum of nonnegative integers. Hence
\[
x>0,\qquad y>0. \tag{11}
\]

By (10), \(P\) divides both \(x\) and \(y\), so it divides their gcd:
\[
P\mid g.
\]
Since \(g>0\) by (11), and \(P=195318521017\geq2\), it follows that
\[
g\geq P\geq2. \tag{12}
\]
Also, by the elementary defining property of a gcd, \(g\mid x\) and \(g\mid y\), hence
\[
g\mid s. \tag{13}
\]
Furthermore, \(g\leq y\), while \(x>0\), and therefore
\[
g\leq y<x+y=s. \tag{14}
\]
By (13), the quotient
\[
q=\frac{s}{g}
\]
is an integer, and (14) implies
\[
q\geq2. \tag{15}
\]

Now consider the next term, whose index is \(3775+K\). Its two preceding terms are exactly \(y=a_{3774+K}\) and \(x=a_{3773+K}\). Thus the actual defining recurrence of A355898 gives
\[
a_{3775+K}=g+\frac{s}{g}=g+q. \tag{16}
\]
On the other hand, the conjectured recurrence (1), which we assumed to hold at every index at least \(3775\), gives at the same index
\[
a_{3775+K}=1+y+x=1+s=1+gq, \tag{17}
\]
where the final equality uses \(s=gq\), valid by (13).

Equating (16) and (17) yields
\[
g+q=1+gq.
\]
Rearranging,
\[
(g-1)(q-1)=0. \tag{18}
\]
But (12) and (15) say that both \(g-1\) and \(q-1\) are positive integers. Their product cannot be zero, contradicting (18).

Therefore the identity \(a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}\) cannot hold for every \(n\geq3775\). The OEIS conjecture asserts, for every such \(n\), a conjunction whose first component is precisely that identity. Since its first component already cannot hold universally, the full three-formula conjecture is false.
